title: Level 3 (Advanced) - D-30
notes:
West leads the ♥10 against 6NT. West is unlikely to have led from the ♥K against 6NT, but playing the ♥A is very unlikely to gain and to refuse the heart finesse would be fatal if West does have the ♥K and the ♦K is with East. In the actual layout East wins the ♥K and returns a heart to the dummy's ♥A.

The diamond finesse is required, but it would be a mistake to finesse in diamonds more than once at this stage. Suppose South crosses in clubs to take two diamond finesses. Both finesses win, but when East discards on the second round of diamonds, West's remaining diamonds stop the suit and there is no way for South to come to 12 tricks.

When West was dealt 4 (or more) diamonds to the ♦K, South's only chance is to hope that West was also dealt the sole defensive club guard. If this is the case then it is possible to squeeze West for a 12th trick.

South takes the first diamond finesse, running the ♦9. When the first finesse succeeds, that is a good sign! In order for the squeeze to mature it is necessary to run the spades before taking the second diamond finesse. When South plays the ♥Q, West is squeezed in the minors.

If West discards a diamond, South will be able to run the diamond suit after taking a second finesse. If, instead of a diamond, West discards a club on the ♥Q, South's clubs will run and it won't matter how many diamonds West was dealt (as long as he was dealt the ♦K).

Many players consider the squeeze to be a technique used only by experts. As this deal illustrates, executing a squeeze sometimes involves little more than declarer playing his winners in the proper order. All basic squeeze positions require an entry to the hand opposite the last side suit winners (South's hearts and spades in this deal). Playing a second round of diamonds too early in the play destroys this entry, making it impossible for the squeeze to succeed.
